specAnchors.text: describe an experiment to prepare a pure,dry sample of a soluble salt,starting from an insoluble reactant
practical:prepare a sample of pure,dry hydrated copper(II)sulfate crystals starting from copper(II)oxide

primer.text: You already know from Acids, Alkalis & Titrations that acids react with bases to form salts and water. This practical puts that reaction to work in the laboratory: an insoluble base, copper(II) oxide, is stirred into warm acid until the acid is used up, and the salt it forms is recovered as blue crystals. Every step you will follow exists to keep that product pure and dry.

modules.title: Method
modules.opening: This practical makes a familiar blue salt from two simple starting materials: an acid and an insoluble black base. The first stage covers the reaction itself, from warming the acid to adding copper(II) oxide until it is in excess. Filtering then removes the leftover solid, leaving a clean blue solution behind.
keyPoints: The aim is a pure, dry batch of hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, made from copper(II) oxide.
Warming the dilute sulfuric acid gently speeds up the reaction with the base.
Copper(II) oxide is added slowly to the hot acid and stirred until it is in excess.
Being in excess means the base stops dissolving and a suspension forms in the acid.
Filtering removes the excess solid base, leaving the salt solution in the evaporating basin.

low.restatement: Warm the dilute acid, stir in copper(II) oxide until some solid will no longer dissolve, then filter the mixture.
low.analogy: It is like making hot chocolate: keep stirring in powder until it piles up undissolved at the bottom, then strain the lumps out.
low.examPointer: Learn the apparatus names as well as the steps; the exam hint singles out apparatus names as a common gap.

medium.restatement: The acid reacts with the insoluble base to form the soluble salt in solution; adding base beyond what reacts guarantees every bit of acid is used up, and filtration then removes the unreacted solid.
medium.analogy: Think of inviting just enough guests to finish the food: you keep adding until some are left standing, which proves the food is all gone.
medium.examPointer: Be ready to explain why the base is added in excess: leftover acid would become dangerously concentrated during evaporation.

modules.title: Results
modules.opening: The second stage turns the blue solution into the crystals the exam asks for. Evaporation concentrates the solution until it is saturated, a cold glass rod confirms the point is reached, and crystallisation is then left to happen on its own. The final crystals should be bright blue and regularly shaped.
keyPoints: The solution is heated gently to evaporate water and make it saturated.
Dipping a cold glass rod into the solution checks saturation, as crystals form on the end.
The filtrate is left in a warm place to dry and crystallise.
Excess solution is decanted away, and the crystals are allowed to dry.
Good crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate are bright blue and regularly shaped.

low.restatement: Heat the filtered solution gently to saturate it, test with a cold glass rod, then leave it to crystallise and dry.
low.analogy: It is like reducing a soup until a spoonful coats the spoon: the cold rod is your taste test, and crystals forming mean the liquid can hold no more.
low.examPointer: Describe the crystals as bright blue and regularly shaped when asked for the expected results, and know the apparatus used at every stage.

medium.restatement: Gentle heating drives off water until the solution is saturated, which the cold-rod test confirms; slow crystallisation in a warm place follows, then decanting and drying leave the pure hydrated crystals.
medium.analogy: Picture the solution as a crowded train: as water evaporates, the salt can no longer all fit in solution, so it steps out in an orderly line as crystals.
medium.examPointer: Water-bath or electric heating is specified for evaporation; the direct Bunsen flame was only for the initial warming, a distinction worth knowing.

glossary.definition: A crystal containing water molecules within its structure; the blue form of copper(II) sulfate is hydrated.
A substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water; copper(II) oxide is the base here.
Added beyond the amount that reacts; some solid remains undissolved, proving the acid has been used up.
A mixture in which fine solid particles are held in a liquid without dissolving.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by filter paper; the liquid passing through is the filtrate.
Holding as much dissolved salt as possible at that temperature, so crystals can form.
The change of a liquid into a gas at the surface; here it concentrates the salt solution.
The formation of solid crystals from a saturated solution as it cools or dries.
